reviewedBy: Claude Code, scheduled morning run, 19 November 2026
reviewBasis: The full text, read in this run from the open access Europe PMC copy, PMC13745404 (European Journal of Pediatrics, CC BY): abstract, introduction, methods including the sample definitions and variables, the opening of the results including the matched transition samples, the strengths and limitations section and the conclusions. This replaces the abstract only review of 12 November, which held the record because the full text could not be reached.

claims.claim: After adjustment, living in a single parent household was not significantly associated with screen time.
claims.basis: Read in the abstract and results: B = 11.98 minutes a week, 95% CI minus 7.41 to 31.37, multilevel models in 8,471 children with at least two waves.

claims.claim: Moving between two parent and single parent households did not change screen time.
claims.basis: No significant change in 701 children who moved from two parents to one and 278 who moved from one to two, each matched to stable peers. The intervals are very wide (minus 94.48 to 131.39 and minus 247.58 to 148.64 minutes a week), so the study cannot rule out a change of one or two hours a week. Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

claims.claim: Each additional sibling was associated with lower screen time.
claims.basis: B = minus 22.71 minutes a week, 95% CI minus 30.18 to minus 15.25. An association, about twenty minutes a week, not a cause.

claims.claim: The findings describe children's screen use today.
claims.basis: The authors' own limitations: data collected 2006 to 2016, television, video games and computers, and it 'might not fully represent current patterns', including smartphones and streaming. For our customer, whose question is the phone and social media, this is the deciding point.

notQuotable: any figure from this paper: the record is rejected and nothing is cleared
any statement that separation or divorce does not affect children's screens
any statement that siblings reduce screen time
evidenceConfidence: HIGH that the paper says what is written here. LOW as evidence for our parent: parent reported minutes of television, games and computer use from 2006 to 2016, before smartphones reached this age group, Australian, with transition results too imprecise to say anything either way.
limitations: Data collected 2006 to 2016; the authors say it may not represent smartphone, social media or streaming use.
Parent reported screen minutes, subject to recall and social desirability bias.
Quantity only, no content or context, no co viewing.
Waves two years apart, so the timing of a transition and any short term response is missed.
Australian children aged about 6 to 13; nothing on the UK or on teenagers.
Transition estimates have very wide intervals.
contradictoryEvidence: From the same paper: the introduction cites cross sectional work finding higher screen time in single parent homes; this study says that gap is explained by sociodemographic factors, chiefly maternal education. Two readings of the same pattern.
No outside study was read against it in this run.
whatThisDoesNotProve: Anything about phones or social media.
That family change has no effect on children.
That having siblings causes less screen time.
mediaMisrepresentation: Coverage was not searched in this run. None is expected.
gdcBeliefs: Evidence or silence: a null result on pre smartphone data does not speak to the parent we serve.
Connection is the protection is about the relationship, not household shape, and this paper measures neither connection nor the plan.
unresolvedQuestions: A replication on recent LSAC waves or another cohort with smartphone era data would be worth a new record.
